summaries.example: Imagine two friends saying “Snow is white” in different languages. The sentences sound different, but they can share the same information. A proposition is the information or thought expressed. Some philosophers say a proposition is structured: it has parts, such as a thing and a property, joined in an organized way. The sentence “Mia helps Leo” might express a proposition with Mia, helping, and Leo as parts.
summaries.summary: Philosophers use “proposition” for the information expressed by a statement. The English sentence “Snow is white” and a German sentence with the same meaning can express one proposition. Propositions are also what people believe or know, and they can be true, false, possible, or necessary. The entry explains a view that propositions are structured objects with parts. For example, a proposition about one person helping another might include the people and the helping relation. Different theories propose different parts and different ways of connecting them. The entry compares neo-Russellian, structured-intension, algebraic, and pictorial approaches, and also discusses earlier ideas from Frege and Russell. A major contrast is the possible-worlds view, which treats a proposition as the set of worlds where it is true. Structured views can distinguish statements that are true in exactly the same worlds but use different words or arrangements.
key_ideas: Different sentences, including sentences in different languages, can express the same proposition.
Propositions can be what people believe, know, doubt, or say.
Structured-proposition theories disagree about which things are parts and what joins those parts.
One reason to favor structure is that sentences with different meanings can be necessarily true without expressing the very same proposition.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic helps explain how language carries information. It also connects with questions about belief: two people can believe the same thing even when they speak different languages. The theories show that philosophers may agree about what propositions do while disagreeing about what propositions are.

important_terms.definition: The information or thought that a statement expresses. Philosophers often say propositions can be true or false.
The meaning or role something has in a sentence, such as a person named by a name or an action described by a verb.
A proposition that has parts joined together in an organized way.
A way things could have been, used by philosophers to think about possibility and necessity.

questions_to_think_about: Can two very different sentences give exactly the same information?
What parts might be in the proposition expressed by “The bird sees the tree”?
Should two statements that are always true count as the same proposition?
What might join the parts of a proposition together?

summaries.example: Suppose “All bachelors are unmarried” and “All brothers are male siblings” are true in every possible world. A possible-worlds theory may identify both propositions with the same set of worlds. A structured theory can keep them distinct because one proposition includes the semantic value of “bachelor” and the other includes the semantic value of “brother.” The difference matters if we ask what someone believes: knowing one statement need not amount to knowing the other.
summaries.summary: The entry examines the metaphysics of structured propositions: propositions are taken to be complex entities whose constituents are connected in a way that reflects, at least roughly, the structure of the sentences expressing them. Propositions serve several roles. They are what declarative sentences express, what can be true or false, what agents believe or know, and what has modal status such as necessity or contingency. The structured view developed partly in response to identifying propositions with sets of possible worlds. That identification captures modal behavior, but it makes all necessarily equivalent propositions identical; it therefore cannot easily preserve differences relevant to belief or to the semantic values of words. Structured accounts aim to recover such information from propositional constituents or associated structure. The entry surveys several approaches. Neo-Russellian theories use individuals, properties, and relations, often together with direct reference. Structured-intension theories use fine-grained functions or meanings associated with linguistic structure. Algebraic theories build propositions through logical functions. The pictorial approach represents propositions with relational diagrams and different possible orders of construction. The entry also traces related ideas to Frege and Russell, while noting unresolved questions about what unifies a proposition and why it has truth conditions.
key_ideas: Propositions are commonly treated as the primary bearers of truth and falsity and as objects of cognitive attitudes such as belief and knowledge.
Structured theories differ over their constituents and over the relation, operation, or mechanism that unifies them.
The possible-worlds account represents propositions as sets of worlds, but this can identify distinct necessarily equivalent contents.
Neo-Russellian theories commonly treat individuals, properties, and relations as constituents and connect this view with direct reference.
Structured-intension theories use more fine-grained meanings while often distinguishing those meanings from the primary bearers of truth.
Algebraic and pictorial theories offer different ways to construct or represent complex propositions.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue lies at the intersection of metaphysics, semantics, logic, and philosophy of mind. It asks how one content can be shared across languages, how differences in wording can matter to belief, and how sentence structure relates to meaning. It also clarifies why a theory can agree that propositions exist and perform important functions while remaining deeply divided about their ontology.

important_terms.definition: The non-linguistic content expressed by a declarative sentence; it can be true or false and can be an object of belief, knowledge, or doubt.
The value or contribution an expression makes to the content of a sentence, such as an individual, property, or relation.
The view that propositions are complex entities with constituents connected by some structure-producing relation or operation.
A representation of a way things could have been. In possible-worlds semantics, a sentence is evaluated for truth at such worlds.
A function from possible worlds to appropriate extensions; for a sentence, it maps worlds to truth values.
An expression whose referent is fixed as the same object across possible circumstances; direct reference is a stronger claim about how that referent contributes to content.
An expression that contributes its referent directly to the proposition expressed, rather than through a descriptive condition.
An approach in which logical operations or functions combine individuals, properties, relations, or propositions into more complex propositions.

questions_to_think_about: If two sentences are true in every possible world, must they express the same proposition?
Can a theory explain belief differences without making the proposition itself too fine-grained?
What should determine the unity of a proposition: its constituents, a logical operation, language users, or something else?
Does a directly referential name contribute only its referent, or should its mode of presentation also matter?
Should propositions have truth conditions independently of minds and languages?

summaries.example: A student says, “The red kite is above the park.” Another student says the same thing in another language. The sounds differ, but both may express one proposition. Now compare “The red kite is above the park” with “The park is below the red kite.” They may be true in the same situations, yet a structured-proposition theory can say they are different because their parts and arrangement differ. A theory that only records which possible situations make a sentence true may lose that difference.
summaries.summary: A proposition is the content expressed by a declarative sentence. It is not identical with the sentence, because people using different languages can express the same content. Propositions are also what people believe, know, doubt, or assert, and they are the things that are true, false, possible, or necessary. The structured view says that propositions are complex: they contain constituents held together in an organized way that is related to sentence structure. The entry contrasts this with the possible-worlds view, according to which a proposition is a set of possible worlds, or equivalently a function from worlds to truth values. That view handles modal ideas neatly, but it can treat very different necessarily equivalent statements as one proposition. Structured views aim to preserve their differences by including semantic values, logical operations, or other kinds of structure. Neo-Russellian theories use individuals, properties, and relations. Structured-intension theories use more detailed meanings than simple sets of worlds. Algebraic theories construct propositions by applying operations. The pictorial approach uses relational diagrams. The entry also considers how Frege and Russell anticipated parts of these debates.
key_ideas: Propositions are not sentences themselves, since different sentences can express the same proposition.
They are used to explain truth, belief, knowledge, doubt, and modal ideas such as possibility.
Structured-proposition theories disagree about what the constituents are and what creates unity among them.
The possible-worlds approach can make all necessarily equivalent statements express one proposition.
Several modern approaches try to preserve differences in structure or meaning, including neo-Russellian, structured-intension, algebraic, and pictorial theories.
Frege and Russell supplied important earlier models for thinking about propositional parts and their connection.
summaries.why_it_matters: Understanding propositions helps explain why changing the words or order in a statement can matter even when its truth conditions stay the same. It also helps explain why two people can share a belief without sharing a language. More broadly, the debate shows how philosophy studies both what language means and what kinds of things meanings might be.

important_terms.definition: The information expressed by a statement; it is treated as something that can be true or false and can be believed or known.
The contribution an expression makes to meaning, such as an object named by a name or a property supplied by a predicate.
A proposition understood as a complex object made from constituents connected in a particular way.
A way the world might have been, used to explain possibility and necessity.
A function showing how an expression’s extension changes from one possible world to another.
A theory that represents a proposition through logical operations applied to items such as individuals, properties, and relations.
The view that a name or other expression contributes its actual referent directly to propositional content.

questions_to_think_about: Would two statements that are true in every possible situation always mean the same thing?
What might be lost if propositions were only sets of possible worlds?
Should the parts of “Ava trusts Ben” be Ava, trusting, and Ben, or something more complex?
How could language users help give propositions their truth conditions?
Can a picture or diagram represent a proposition better than a list of its parts?
